extraction.name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset for advancing object recognition by placing object recognition in the context of broader scene understanding. The dataset contains images of complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context, with objects labeled using per-instance segmentations for precise localization. It contains 91 object categories (80 with segmentations in the 2014 release) with 2.5 million labeled instances across 328,000 images. The dataset addresses three core research problems: detecting non-iconic views of objects, contextual reasoning between objects, and precise 2D localization of objects.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
extraction.citeAs: Lin, T., Maire, M., Belongie, S., Hays, J., Perona, P., Ramanan, D., Dollár, P., and Zitnick, C. L. (2014). Microsoft COCO: Common objects in context. In ECCV.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Images were gathered from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images. The authors searched for pairwise combinations of object categories (e.g., 'dog + car') to find non-iconic images, and also searched for scene/object category pairs. At most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded. In rare cases where enough images could not be found, they searched for single categories and performed an explicit filtering stage to remove iconic images. Annotation was performed via Amazon Mechanical Turk using a 3-stage pipeline: category labeling, instance spotting, and instance segmentation, followed by a segmentation verification step.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Others
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were collected from Flickr, which contains photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed (detected with GIST descriptors) and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize chance of near-duplicate images existing across splits. An AMT filtering task allowed users to remove invalid or iconic images from a grid of 128 candidates.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation pipeline consisted of 3 primary tasks: (a) category labeling - workers labeled categories present in the image using a hierarchical approach with 11 super-categories, with 8 workers per image; (b) instance spotting - workers placed a cross on top of each instance of a specific category found in the previous stage, up to 10 instances per category per image, with 8 workers per image; (c) instance segmentation - workers segmented each object instance using a modified OpenSurfaces interface. A single worker segmented each instance, but all workers had to complete a training task. Segmentations were then verified by 3-5 workers who judged whether each matched the instance well; segmentations of insufficient quality were discarded. Five written caption descriptions were also added to each image.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT); instance segmentation used a modified interface from the OpenSurfaces project
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Worker precision and recall on category labeling was analyzed by comparing to dedicated expert workers (co-authors). The union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any of the expert workers, with worker recall saturating at around 9-10 AMT workers. Even dedicated experts often disagreed on object presence due to inherent ambiguity. Authors estimated that over 99% of all object categories not rejected as false positives are detected given 8 annotators. For segmentation verification, each segmentation was initially shown to 3 annotators; if any indicated it was bad, it was shown to 2 additional workers. Segmentations not receiving at least 4 of 5 favorable votes were discarded. Workers who consistently produced poor segmentations had all their work discarded.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers for category labeling; 8 workers for instance spotting; 1 worker for instance segmentation with 3-5 workers for segmentation verification; 5 written captions per image
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Dataset was split into two roughly equal parts for faster release. The 2014 release contains 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images. The cumulative 2015 release will contain a total of 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images. Annotations for train and validation data are released, but not for test. The 2014 release was limited to a subset of 80 categories (segmentations not collected for 11 categories). The dataset will evolve and grow over time.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset focuses on 'thing' categories and not 'stuff' categories. Categories were selected based on co-authors' votes considering frequency, usefulness, and diversity. The dataset is limited to entry-level categories commonly used by humans. Dataset was compared against others using Torralba and Efros cross-dataset generalization metric showing MS COCO is more difficult than PASCAL VOC.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The 2014 release does not include segmentations for 11 categories (hat, shoe, eyeglasses, mirror, window, door, street sign, plate, desk, blender, hair brush) due to too many instances, ambiguity, difficulty to label, confusion with other categories, or too few instances. Only 'thing' categories are labeled, not 'stuff' categories which could provide significant contextual information. For images with more than 10-15 object instances of the same category, remaining instances were marked as 'crowds' using a single segment rather than individually segmented.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation. The dataset is designed for detection and segmentation of objects occurring in their natural context, supporting object recognition, bounding box detection, instance segmentation, and contextual reasoning research. Areas marked as crowds are ignored during evaluation and do not affect detector scores.
